doc.title: Allan Vaché interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000

title: Hopes for jazz's future and the lost club training ground
summary: Optimism about jazz, and how club sink-or-swim experience trained him.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Well I wish you the best and I hope in ten years, as you said, that jazz is still healthy enough.
That you are able to keep doing what you’re doing.

You know I have to be somewhat optimistic and say that I think it will, because it’s lasted a lot longer than a lot of people thought it was going to last now, and just hopefully it will appeal to a younger generation — at least maintain the status quo that it has now.

Well it’s become an art form for sure, considered to be an art form of American culture, which is a good thing. Sometimes I wish there was still the club scene that there used to be, at least as far as training grounds.

Yeah. You see I had that. It’s a shame about what there is today because kids coming up really don’t have that any longer. I mean like I can remember going and sitting in clubs when I was a kid, and it was kind of a sink or swim situation and either you learned or you didn’t. Sometimes you weren’t treated so well if you didn’t do too well. But it was a good leaning experience and the next time you showed up you made sure you knew the tune and you were in better shape and better prepared.
